files.start_heading: ### Additional detail relocated from the Methods
files.replacement:
### Crosswalk coverage, the food-insecurity measure, and predictor coding

Supports the Methods section Predictors and Harmonization.

The crosswalk available when the protocol amendment was written and locked held a 175-variable extract, of which the seventeen predictors are every eligible concept; the predictor set is thus exhaustive with respect to that extract rather than with respect to the full crosswalk. A later exhaustive extraction identified 265 variables common to both NHANES cycles, and the five further harmonizable items screened post hoc against NHANES outcome associations came from that extraction.

A direct Korea-US comparison using the same 18-item household food-security module found food insecurity associated with higher odds of PHQ-9 depression in both countries, with a larger association in Korea [31]. The single-item KCHS measure used here is therefore the weakest link in the harmonized set rather than a difference in the underlying construct.

The three ordinal scores were modeled as numeric variables rather than as unordered categories, an ordinal coding rather than a set of indicator columns. Recomputation of the income quintile within each dataset and, inside KCHS, within each survey year is the one preprocessing step not carried over from the development training set unchanged, the underlying income instruments not being on a common scale across the two surveys or across KCHS years.

### Comparability of the two algorithm searches and the parsimony procedure

Supports the Methods section Model Development and Evaluation.

The training set's approximately 1,000 events per candidate predictor is far above conventional events-per-predictor requirements. Only gradient boosting received the preceding feature-representation and hyperparameter search, hence the algorithm comparison is like-for-like at each algorithm's tuned best configuration rather than equal in cumulative search effort. The four candidate interaction terms did not improve cross-validated discrimination.

Both algorithm searches used individual-level cross-validation, and the selection step may therefore be mildly optimistic; the reported performance rests instead on the cluster-level separation of the internal hold-out and of the parsimony selection set and is unaffected.

Predictor order and item count were both fixed inside the development training set, split into a 450,000-record fitting set and a 50,000-record selection set. Predictors were entered in descending order of global SHAP importance, the model was refitted at every item count from 1 to 17, and the count was chosen on selection-set AUROC by the analysis plan's margin, the smallest set within 0.02 AUROC of the full model.

### Decision-curve construction, intended use, and deployment requirements

Supports the Methods section External Validation and Sensitivity Analyses.

Each dataset carries its own screen-all and screen-none default strategies in the decision-curve analysis, and the reported net benefit is therefore internal to each cohort (Table S5 in Multimedia Appendix 1).

The model is intended as a triage aid for population-level screening programs and web or mobile self-assessment services, operated by public-health and primary-care services rather than by individuals acting alone, to prioritize who receives a full PHQ-9 and clinical follow-up.

Deployment presupposes local recalibration and, the household income predictor being a within-cohort rank, a local income distribution to rank against.

files.start_heading: ### Discussion detail relocated from the manuscript (utility, deployment, and limitations)
files.replacement:
### Sample composition and the complete-case restriction

Supports Results Participant Characteristics.

The contrast between the development and external samples in body mass index, food insecurity and outcome frequency is consistent with genuinely distinct populations and, for food insecurity, with the single-item-versus-module measurement difference recorded in the harmonization crosswalk.

Respondents missing only one or two depression items can be recovered by filling the missing items with the person-mean. That change moved the observed prevalence by no more than 0.1 percentage points in either cycle (unweighted: 9.23% to 9.27% pre-pandemic, 12.69% to 12.78% post-pandemic), indicating that the complete-case restriction does not itself shift the observed outcome frequency. Item-level counts are in Table S1 in Multimedia Appendix 1.

### Predictor attribution and the alcohol-definition sensitivity analysis

Supports Results Interpretability, Fairness, and Clinical Utility and Results Sensitivity Analyses.

Food insecurity ranked 10th by mean absolute SHAP value in KCHS but 8th in NHANES pre-pandemic; the item is a single question in KCHS against the 10-item module in NHANES.

Replacing current drinking with drinking at least twice weekly, with binge drinking, or with all three indicators together reached 0.769-0.771 pre-pandemic and 0.770 post-pandemic against an in-run baseline of 0.772 and 0.769; that run predates the data-integrity corrections and the cluster-level split, hence its levels are not comparable with the primary estimates or with Table S6 in Multimedia Appendix 1.

### Clinical utility of the six-item form and the conditions on its use

Supports Discussion Clinical and Policy Implications and Discussion Strengths and Limitations.

Operating characteristics support the usefulness claim, which rests on a decision-analytic criterion rather than on a nominal AUROC cut-off.

The mobile-delivery evidence cited in Principal Findings [40] concerns intervention delivery to defined patient groups, and no equivalent trial evidence exists for a transported screening algorithm.

Item reduction should be re-evaluated whenever the deployment population differs materially from the development population, given that the ranking of predictors that supports a six-item form is itself population-dependent.

Equity requires explicit and continuing monitoring rather than an assumption that the development-time estimate holds [45].

The limitations set out in Strengths and Limitations are given in descending order of consequence.

files.start_heading: ### Discussion detail relocated from the manuscript (ceiling, oracle, and calibration)
files.replacement:
### Between-cycle stability and the in-domain oracle comparison

Supports Discussion Plausible Mechanisms for the External Ceiling.

The width of the between-cycle difference interval leaves moderate change in either direction admissible; within that limit the data are consistent with no decay across the population-wide shock that motivated the analysis.

The oracle comparison is pooled across cycles while the transported estimates are cycle-specific, and the intervals overlap; it therefore locates the limit in the predictors rather than in the transfer only to the extent that the oracle is a fair upper bound.

Each of the two specification analyses that locate the shortfall alters the target condition or the population as well as the gap, hence the pattern is suggestive rather than confirmatory.

The interpretability comparison is a statement about the fixed model's attribution and not about the external predictor-outcome associations, which the attribution never observes.

### Leakage control and the training-set size result

Supports Results Testing Whether External Discrimination Can Be Raised Above ~0.77.

Leakage is the failure mode that has driven reproducibility problems across machine-learning-based science [42]; runs screened on external labels are identified as such in Table S11 in Multimedia Appendix 1.

That increasing the training set from 0.5 to 2 million records slightly lowered external discrimination is a pattern consistent with source-specific overfitting rather than with an estimation-limited ceiling.

### Development-survey coverage of multimorbidity and healthcare utilization

Supports Discussion Strengths and Limitations.

Beyond hypertension and diabetes, dyslipidemia, osteoporosis, cataract and arthritis are fielded in a single KCHS year and therefore cannot enter a model pooled over 2017-2025. KCHS collects no broader chronic-disease inventory, no hospitalization record and no visit counts, and a development survey that captured multimorbidity and utilization might raise the attainable ceiling.

### Prior Korean models and the contribution of the present study

Supports Discussion Comparison With Prior Work.

Both prior Korean models identified perceived stress and subjective health as dominant predictors, and neither attempted external validation. The contribution of the present study over that work includes an explicit transportability ceiling characterized by an in-domain oracle and a catalogued set of over two thousand leakage-controlled runs.

### Recalibration of the transported probabilities

Supports Results External Validation Across Country and Pandemic Period.

Each intercept-plus-slope update used the full sample of the cohort it was fitted in, and the local sample size needed for a stable update was not examined here.

Temperature scaling, the third of the three pre-specified recalibration steps applied out-of-sample, left less residual miscalibration than intercept-only updating: the calibration slope was 0.83 pre-pandemic and 1.17 post-pandemic, the post-pandemic value overshooting 1 rather than lying between the intercept-only (0.68) and intercept-plus-slope (1.00) results, with calibration-in-the-large +0.02 and -0.02. Intercept-plus-slope updating remains the recommended deployment update.

verdict: PASS with three cross-reference fixes. FACTS: every fact in the eight current blocks survives in a replacement or in docs/manuscript_17var.md; all 32 declared deletions verified at their claimed homes (notably the denominator argument and 14.3%/32.7% in the untouched Table S1 caption and rows, appendix3 lines 7/15/17; the 0.003 harmonization ceiling in the untouched Table S7 caption, line 148; the 0.0046-against-0.005 tie-band note in the untouched Table S2 deviation row, line 54; "selected main effects" at manuscript line 99; the 500,000/100,001/2,048,510 split at manuscript line 45; the six-item burden and symptom-item claims at manuscript lines 166 and 208; the three monitoring quantities with [45] at manuscript line 212; the multimorbidity list and coverage conclusion in the untouched appendix4 Interpretation bullet and footnote, lines 7 and 9). Three facts dropped without being declared - "The parsimonious form places a low-burden self-report instrument within reach for digital triage", "Whether triage delivered this way improves depression outcomes was not evaluated here", and the development-fixed-operating-point net-benefit sentence - all three survive at manuscript lines 190, 226 and 182 and in the untouched appendix3 Interpretation paragraph, so no fact is lost. NUMBERS: no numeric value, CI, variable name or sample size vanished; every value kept is character-identical to the current text (0.83/1.17/0.68/1.00/+0.02/-0.02; 9.23/9.27/12.69/12.78; 0.769-0.771/0.770/0.772/0.769; 175/265/1,000/450,000/50,000/0.02; 0.5 to 2 million). PROCESS LANGUAGE: all eleven headings name a subject; no sentence mentions trimming, revision, relocation, condensing or editing history; all five boilerplate sentences and all "No new result is introduced" trailers are gone. REFERENCES: [31], [40], [42], [45] all resolve, and the newly added [42] (Kapoor and Narayanan, leakage and the reproducibility crisis in machine-learning-based science) matches its sentence exactly; every table pointer uses the item-first/appendix-last grammar; all named manuscript sections exist. STYLE: no banned pronoun, no "because", no result-clause "so", no "ie,"/"eg,", no em dash, en dash or Unicode minus, no P value, no bold run-in label, US spelling throughout. Region boundaries as proposed are correct for all three files.
